newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE - Ghinwa Bhutto carries slain husband's torch.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ghinwa Bhutto carries slain husband's torch.

text.p: Ghinwa Bhutto, elegant Lebanese-born widow of Benazir Bhutto's slain brother Murtaza, is standing against her Iranian-born mother-in-law Nusrat in one of the most bizarre contests of Pakistan's elections.
The two women competing for votes on February 3 are reluctant rivals, caught up in a complex Bhutto family feud in which any ideological differences are irrelevant.
"That particular seat belongs to Murtaza and his heir should get it," Ghinwa said of her NA-164 constituency in the Bhutto heartland of Larkana in the southern province of Sindh.
Ghinwa, 34, says she loves Nusrat, but has been unable to contact her since President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir's government on November 5, alleging corruption and misrule.

"I would like to see my mother-in-law and ask whether she is really serious in contesting elections against me," Ghinwa told Reuters in an interview. "I know my mother-in-law is very ill and the children are dying to see her."
GRIEF

Nusrat, who has already lost her husband Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and younger son Shahnawaz to violent deaths, is grief-stricken at Murtaza's killing by Karachi police on September 20 and has remained tightly closeted in Benazir's entourage since then.
Ghinwa herself is no stranger to political violence. Her family moved to Syria from her native Tripoli after Lebanon's civil war erupted in 1975 when she was 13.
She met Murtaza in Damascus, where he was living in exile, through his daughter Fatima, now 14, who was attending the school where Ghinwa taught Arabic. They married in 1989.
Fatima is the offspring of Murtaza's first marriage to the daughter of a former Afghan foreign minister.
"Actually, Fatima introduced me to Murtaza. I don't know whether I love Murtaza for Fatima or Fatima for Murtaza," said Ghinwa, who bore Murtaza a son, Zulfikar, in 1991.
In Urdu, Zulfikar means sword, the election symbol of former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was executed in 1979 on the orders of late military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.

Ghinwa plunged into the maelstrom of Pakistani politics after her husband's still unexplained murder, laying claim to the mantle of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) founded by Bhutto, the father of Benazir and Murtaza, in 1967.

Ghinwa took over leadership of the PPP-Shaheed Bhutto faction, formed by Murtaza as a challenge to Benazir, whom he blamed for failing to waive charges that kept him in jail for several months after his 1993 return from 17 years in exile.
HUSBAND FACES CHARGES

Benazir's husband Asif Ali Zardari is facing charges linking him with Murtaza's killing. He denies any involvement. Benazir says her husband had no hand in the murder, which she describes as a conspiracy against her government and the Bhutto family.
Ghinwa said she lived in fear after Murtaza's death and had asked Leghari to post paramilitary rangers outside her home.
"I have entered politics at the unanimous demand of Murtaza's followers," said Ghinwa, who took Pakistani nationality only after her husband's death.
"I love Pakistan. Pakistan is my country. I want an end to exploitation of the poor...a society based on justice. I want to fulfil my husband's mission," she said.

"I did not know the people loved Murtaza so much. People also love me as a symbol of Murtaza, who wanted to complete the mission of his father -- Roti, Kapra aur Makan (bread, clothing and shelter) for the people," she added.
"Our first priority will be to get rid of our loans and debts, revive our industry, increase our exports, provide new job opportunities and revive agriculture," Ghinwa said.
She waved V-for-victory signs during Murtaza's 1993 campaign campaign, but previously stayed out of politics, feeling handicapped by her poor Urdu language skills.
A fluent speaker of English, French and Arabic, she is now learning Urdu and has begun to use it at election rallies.
"I will not be able to say how many seats we will win, but we are aiming for a lot," she said, adding that her party would have preferred more time to prepare for elections.
Ghinwa, a pale, dark-haired woman, wears typical Pakistani shalwar kameez outfits of long shirt over trousers, favouring black or white, with a white Islamic headscarf.
She likes cooking and gardening and keeps a small menagerie of peacocks, deer, parrots and ducks. "This is my hobby," she smiles.
